summary: On December 25, 2023, the President of India signed the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita Act, which was passed by Parliament in the Seventy-fourth Year of the Republic of India. The Act consolidates and amend the provisions relating to offences and for matters connected therewith. The provisions of the Act will be applicable to all offences committed outside of India, including those committed by persons in the service of the Government of India and those who are not citizens of the country. It also provides for the punishment of those who commit a crime in the course of serving in the military or in the services of the government of India or who are found to have committed a crime while serving. In the event that a person is found guilty under the provisions of this Act, he or she will be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years, or to a fine of not less than Rs.12,000, or both. The penalty for a person convicted under the Act for a crime committed outside India will be the same as that for an offence committed within India. In addition, the provisions will apply to any person on any ship or aircraft registered in India where it may be, or for any person in any place outside India, who commits an offence targeting a computer resource located in India. The Supreme Court of India has ruled that the West Bengal Industrial Tribunal was wrong to order a company to pay a bonus to its workmen who had been paid at the rate of one month's wages for more than 30 years. The workmen claimed that the sole object of the bonus was to meet expenses and that the payment of this bonus had become customary and a term of employment. The Court held that the appellant had made it clear that the payments from 1948 to 1952 were ex gratia and that they were entitled to puja bonus on the basis that it was a customary and traditional payment. The court also held that there was no evidence that the company had made any misrepresentation of the terms of the agreement. The appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal and the matter was referred to the High Court of West Bengal for further proceedings. The Supreme court has directed the Industrial Tribunal to set aside the order of the Second Industrial Tribunal, West Bengal, which ordered the company to make a payment of Rs. 2,50,000 to the workmen. The decision was made by Justices Jasti, S.P. Sinha, P. B. Gajanandkar and K. N. Wanehoo of the Supreme Court on May 7, 1959 and was published on May 8, 1959.

The Supreme Court has dismissed an appeal by a group of Indian sugar manufacturers against a ruling by the High Court of India in a similar case. The Court held that the Sugar Export Promotion Act, 1958, was constitutionally valid. The petitioners had challenged the constitutionality of the Act, which was enacted for the purpose of exporting sugar with a view to earning foreign exchange. The High Court had held that it was not in the public interest to increase the price of sugar for internal sales by 50 per cent to enable the owners to recoup the loss suffered by them by the delivery of the sugar for export. The Petitioners challenged the unconstitutionality of this provision in the Court of Appeal, which ruled that it did not violate the fundamental rights of the petitioners under the Constitution of India. The Case was referred to the Supreme Court for further consideration after the Court of Appeal had dismissed the appeal by the petitioners.

The Supreme Court has upheld the award of a profit bonus to the employees of The Tata Oil Mills Ltd., Mazdoor Sangh, Howrah, Bombay, for the year 1955-56. The award was made by the Industrial Tribunal of Bombay in a dispute between the company and its workmen. The dispute arose over a demand for payment of a sum equivalent to four months' wages/salary for all employees of less than Rs. 500 per mansem. The appellant was entitled to a 4 per cent return on the depreciation reserve used as working capital. The tribunal held that the appellant had not proved that the items of income were the result of the direct efforts of labour in the bonus. The court held that it was not necessary to establish direct connection between the efforts of the workmen and each item of profit earned. It was not income in the normal course of business as it1as not likely to arise again. It had arisen out of fortuitous stances and had nothing whatsoever to do with the effort of labour. The Court held that there was no need for the appellant to prove that the profit of Rs. 3 lacs due to change in the method of valuation was real profit due to the efforts and efforts of Jabour and should not be taken into account. The appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal. The judgment was delivered by Justices C.J. Das, N.H. Grewal, P. Gajanandar and K.N. Wan

The High Court of Allahabad has issued a final order on a complaint filed by the Chief Justice of the Allahabad High Court against a senior judge of the High Court for allegedly violating the rules and regulations of the court. The order was passed by Justice S. Devi Kumar Jain, who was then the Chief Judge of the Family Court. The complaint alleged that Kumar had violated the rules of the Court by failing to comply with the provisions of the Rules and Regulations of the Supreme Court and Rules of Court of Justices of the Bombay and Calcutta and Rules and Regulation of Court Rules of the Calcutta and Bombay High Court. Kumar also allegedly violated the Rules of High Court by not complying with certain provisions of Rules and Rules. The final order, which was issued on October 2, 2016, orders Kumar to pay a fine of Rs.12,000 and further orders him to pay costs of Rs,50,000. The Court also ordered Kumar to submit a copy of the final order by October 10, 2016. The order is subject to further orders by the Court.

The Reserve Bank of India ( RBI) today announced the appointment of Charulatha S. Kar as Executive Director (ED) with effect from July 1, 2024. Kar was previously serving as Chief General Manager-in-Charge in the Human Resource Management Department. Kar has over three decades of experience in the Reserve Bank having worked in areas of Payment and Settlement Systems, Information Technology, Government Banking, Internal accounts and Human Resource management. As Executive Director, Kar will look after the Department of Communication, Human Resources Management Department, and Right to Information (First Appellate Authority). Kar is a post-graduate in commerce from University of Mumbai and Diploma in Treasury & Forex management. She is also a Certified Associate of IIBF.

The Central Government has issued new rules for the maintenance of records of the nature and value of transactions, the procedure and manner of maintaining and time for furnishing of information and verification of the identity of the clients of the banking companies, financial institutions and intermediaries, namely, the Aadhaar number, the name of the client and the name and address of the reporting entity. The new rules come into force on the date of their publication in the Official Gazette. The rules provide for the use of the "Central Know Your Customer" (KYC) system, which is being implemented by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), to identify and verify the identity and transactions of the customers of the banks, financial services companies and intermediaries. The RBI has issued a guidance to all banks, banks and intermediaries on how to use the "KYC" system. The guidance provides that the reporting entities must comply with the provisions of these rules and the rules of the Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA) and the Banking Rules, 2005. The guidance also provides that there is no obligation for the reporting companies to provide the client with the information. The reporting entities will be required to maintain records of all transactions, including those involving the client's bank account, and to provide such information to the client in a manner that is consistent with the requirements of the PMLA and the Bank Rules. The Securities and Exchange Board of India has charged two former members of the Calcutta Stock Exchange with insider trading in the shares of DSQ Industries Ltd., formerly known as Lexus Exports Ltd. The Board has also charged Harish Gopal Biyani and Amritlal Balasaria, who are also former members, for their roles in the alleged insider trading. According to the SEC's complaint, filed on March 31, 2019, DSQ's share price increased significantly from November 1, 2000 to January 1, 2001 when the company's stock price rose significantly. The complaint further alleges that, from November 2000 to March 2001, Harish Biyani engaged in a pattern of manipulative trading in shares of the company by acting as an intermediary between two brokers, acting as a broker for the purpose of raising the price of the stock and acting as the intermediary for the purchase and sale of the shares. The SEC alleges that the two brokers engaged in the manipulative trading by acting on the basis of false and misleading information provided by the company in its distribution schedule filed with the CSE. The Commission's investigation was conducted by Sanjay Kumar and Sanjay Kumar of the Market Abuse Unit, and supervised by Prashant Kumar and Anup Kumar. The settlement is subject to approval by the Board of Directors of the CSE and the Court of Appeal.

The Supreme Court has ruled that the Industrial Tribunal of Assam was not competent to hear an appeal by a worker dismissed for gross misconduct. The Court held that the Tribunal was not a tribunal under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and that the basic principle of natural justice was that the opponent must be given the opportunity of questjoning the witnesses after knowing in full what they had to state against him. The Tribunal held in favour of the workman and ordered that he should be reinstated. The appeal was filed by the Assam Chah Karmchari Sangh, a registered trade union, which was represented by B.N. Ghosh and K. P. Gtpta, for the appellant Phulbari Tea Estate Co. Ltd.

The Supreme Court of India has upheld the payment of overtime wages to employees of the Central Railway Workshop and Factory, Parel, Bombay, under the Payment of Wages Act, 1936. The Court held that the workers were entitled to overtime wages under the Act even if they were not workers within the meaning of the Factories Act. The Act provides for overtime wages for employees in all establishments, including factories, and the workers in these establishments are entitled to claim the overtime wages as provided for by the Act. In the case of the respondents, the Court found that only four of them were required to do the work of progress timekeepers and the rest were merely employees. The Authority accepted the alternative case made by the respondents and directed the appellant to file a statement showing the overtime pay due to each of them and ordered it to pay the same. The judgment of the Court was delivered by Gajdragadkar J. Gajanandkar, Justice of the High Court of Bombay and held that, on a proper construction of s. 70 of the Act, it is clear that the first part of the section excludes a factory and its employees from the operation of the act. The second part makes the relevant provisions of the Bombay Shops and Establishments Act applicable to them. The court held that it was not correct to say that the Act does not apply to the workers of the workshop. The decision of the Authority was upheld by a majority of the judges of the Supreme Court.

The Supreme Court of India has ruled that an individual who filed a voluntary return for a period of four years after the end of the period of notice under the Income-tax Act, 1922, was entitled to a refund of the amount of the return. The Act requires every person whose total income exce'ed the niaximum amount not be charged to file a return for the period ending on December 31, 1950. The period of the notice was four years. The appellant, H.ANCHHODDAS KARSONDAS, claimed that he had not disclosed any taxable income and had not filed a return under the proviso to s. 34(1) of the Act. The Court held that the appellant had not taken advantage of the time allowed under this proviso and that the return was invalid. The court also held that, since the appellant did not disclose any of the information in the return, he was not entitled to the refund. The appeal was filed by Mr. KarsonDAS and Mr. Bombay, who claimed that they had not been informed of the date of the public notice and that they were not required to file the returns. The Appeal was dismissed by the Court and the matter was referred to the High Court for further consideration. The Supreme court held that Mr.KarsonDAS had not violated the provisions of the Income Tax Act and the Act and ordered him to pay the amount due. The High Court also ordered the appellant to pay a fine of Rs. 2,50,000.

The Constitution of India was amended on 1 May, 2024 by the Government of India through the Constitution (One Hundred and Sixth Amendment) Act, 2023. The amended Constitution provides for the following: The right of citizenship of certain persons who have migrated to India from Pakistan. The right to be a citizen of India is also guaranteed by the Constitution. The Constitution also provides for a right to education and the right to freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion. The amendment to the Constitution also includes the right of the Indian citizen to be able to apply for a passport and to be registered as a member of a political party. The amendments to the amended Constitution also provide for the appointment of the Chief Justice of India and the Chief Minister of the State where there is a conflict of interest between the two. The provisions of the Constitution provide that the President of the Republic of India can be appointed as a Member of the Parliament of India. The President of India has the power to appoint the Chief Ministers of the States where there are any political or territorial disputes. The new Constitution provides that the Prime Minister of India will be the President and the President will have the power of Parliament to make recommendations to the President for the approval or disapproval of the President.

The Calcutta High Court has dismissed an appeal by two former directors of a Calcutta-based company against a tax charge imposed by the Income-tax Tribunal for failing to disclose that they had received payments from the company. The tribunal had found that the directors had agreed to pay off a portion of the tax charge to avoid disclosure of misfeasance by the company's managing agents. The directors claimed that the amount they received should be excluded from their tax bill, and that the payments were made for the purpose of carrying on the business, and not for the benefit of the company itself. The court found that, in fact, the payments had been made to the managing agents for the purposes of carrying out their duties. The Court found that there was no evidence that the payment was made for any purpose other than to cover the directors' expenses. The High Court agreed with the Tribunal's findings and dismissed the appeal. The appeal was dismissed by the Chief Justice of the High Court. The case has been referred to the Supreme Court of India for further consideration.

The Supreme Court of India has acquitted a businessman convicted under the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 for allegedly violating the provisions of the Act. The Act was passed by the Bihar legislature in 1950 and was intended to abolish the state's zamindaries and provide for compensation for land acquired by the state for development projects. The businessman had challenged the Act in the Patna High Court, claiming that the Act was unconstitutional. The Court agreed with his argument and held that there was no need for the Act to be re-enacted. The High Court had held that it was not necessary to re-examine the Act because the provisions in the Act were constitutional and valid. The court also held that the businessman had not proved that he had violated the provisions under the Act by failing to pay compensation for the land acquired. The high court held that he was acquitted on the ground that he did not breach the Act's provisions and that the trial court had not found him guilty of any offence under the provisions.

The Calcutta High Court has upheld the conviction of a West Bengal man for attempting to take out of India notes out of the country. The appellant was arrested by the customs authorities at the Bengal Aerodrome on September 7, 1952 and charged with an offence under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1952. On September 16, 1952, the Reserve Bank of India authorised the Additional District Magistrate, West Bengal, to proceed against the appellant. The Magistrate granted the appellant bail and allowed his application for reduction of security and fixed the trial for March 26, and 27 for evidence. The trial was held on February 2, 1953, and the Magistrate found the appellant guilty of the offence and sentenced him to two years in prison. The High Court held that the trial was without jurisdiction as the Magistrate had taken cognizance of the alleged offence on September 16, 1952 without there being a complaint in writing. The Court also held that there was no need for the trial to be held on the date of the complaint as the complaint was filed and the case was valid. The court held that it was not necessary to hold the trial on the same day as the alleged offences as the case had been filed and that the Magistrate was entitled to issue a warrant of arrest for the purpose of the trial. The high court also found that the charges against the accused were not proved against him.

The Supreme Court of India has upheld the conviction of a man convicted of murdering a woman in Calcutta in 1955. The Court held that the trial judge had correctly directed the jury that the evidence of an approver must satisfy a double test: that he must be a reliable witness and his evidence must receive sufficient corroboration and that the corroborating evidence was not sufficient to connect the appellant with the crime. In the present case there was no evidence to show that the approver's evidence was in any way unreliable. The High Court had dismissed the appellant's appeal against his conviction. The appeal has been refused. The Appeal is being heard by Justices G. Chandra Bhat, J.L. Karpur, and Justices J.M. Ghosh and P.K. Ghosh.

The Supreme Court has allowed an appeal by the former managing director of the Tata Oil Mills Ltd. against an award by the Appellate Tribunal of Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) against him for his role in the liquidation of Great Indian Motor Works Ltd.<n>The Tribunal held that no relationship of employer and employee existed between the auction-purchaser and the discharged employees who had been discharged prior to the purchase of the business. The Tribunal directed the liquidators to pay compensation to the discharged workers. The liquidators were refused sanction to appeal from the said award, by the High Court, whereupon the auctioneer preferred an appeal in the name of the company represented by himself as the managing director prior to its liquidation. The High Court dismissed the appeal in limine as incompetent in view of the provisions of s. 457 of the Companies Act 1956, on the ground that the appeal was not maintainable as it was not authorised by the high court. The Court held that the Tribunal's decision was not inconsistent with the judgment and order of the Court of Appeal in the same case. The appeal was allowed by a majority of three judges, Justices G. Chandrasekhar, J. Chandrasena and J. Mukundar. The court also ordered the parties to bear their own costs. The decision was made by Justices Chandrasegar, Chandrasandra and J Chandrashara of the Supreme Court on May 6th, 2016.

The Supreme Court has dismissed an appeal by an Indian company against an order of the Labour Court ordering it to pay a group of workers a total of 1,800 in back pay and interest. The appeal was filed by the workers, who had been employed by M/s. M.M. Ispahani Ltd., which shortly before the partition of India transferred its registered office from CO:Icutta to Chittagong. The workmen were originally employed by the company, which used to pay them at the rate of one month's wages and the appellant also paid the same from 1948 up to 1952 even in the years in which the appellant suffered losses. The workers claimed that they were entitled to the bonus as it was an implied term of the employment of the workmen. The tribunal held that the workers were not entitled to any benefits arising out of their employment with M/S. M's.<n>The Court held that there was no express or implied under-taking regarding continuity of service when employing the workers.
